intro: Bamberg's protected trees are not headline giants: eight of the nine carry no measured age, and the registers describe most in a single line. What they have is open ground: a spring path above Wildensorg, a roadside lane, a demolished manor's site, a riverbank downstream, Kilian's oak at a junction in Schesslitz, field trees outside Dörfleins, Unterhaid and Pödeldorf, and toward Teuchatz a lime thick enough that people once thought it was three trees fused together. If you carry a tape measure, we would like to hear from you.
meta_description: Nine protected trees around Bamberg: limes by a hillside spring, Kilian's oak at Schesslitz, a village maple and a legend-dated lime near Teuchatz.
question_answer: The closest thing to a dated tree is the Great Lime of Teuchatz, well outside the city itself, whose girth points to something like 350 to 400 years if a local legend about its planting is right: soldiers buried here during the Thirty Years' War, sometime in the 1630s. None of the other eight protected trees here carries any age estimate at all. The registers give only a location and a protected status for those eight. If you know how old any of these nine actually are, tell us.
question_meta: Nine protected trees around Bamberg; the closest to a dated one is a lime near Teuchatz, its girth suggesting 350 to 400 years by legend.
question_context: Bamberg's Naturdenkmal-Verordnung, passed in November 1995 and amended in 2007, protects trees across the city and its outskirts and dates almost none of them. Each entry carries a number, a name, a location and the fact of protection, nothing about planting dates. Three of the first four stand within a kilometre and a half of each other on the hillside above Wildensorg: two limes by a spring, an oak on the Teufelsgraben, and a lime on a demolished manor's site. The fourth stands alone by the Regnitz in Bug. None of those four carries a girth measurement. The fifth, the Great Lime of Teuchatz, stands sixteen kilometres out on a road with no rail and no confirmed bus, documented instead by a dedicated Wikipedia article citing published dendrology surveys, and it is the only one of the nine anyone has ever measured: 770 centimetres round in 1990, 822 in 2008. The sixth, the Kilianseiche in Schesslitz, comes from the district's 2009 ordinance, which records its name and place and not even a species. Three more, a maple at Dörfleins and limes at Unterhaid and Pödeldorf, come from the same district list, named only maple and lime.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bamberg?
faq.a: The best estimate belongs to the Great Lime of Teuchatz, a satellite tree well outside Bamberg, whose girth points to somewhere between 350 and 400 years if a local legend about its planting during the Thirty Years' War is right. None of the trees standing within the city itself has been dated at all.

faq.q: Can I see all nine trees in one walk?
faq.a: No. Three, the Ottobrunnen lindens, the Teufelsgraben oak and the Rothof linden, sit within about a kilometre and a half of each other on the Wildensorg hillside. The Buger Hof linden is a separate trip a few kilometres away on the Regnitz. The Great Lime of Teuchatz is sixteen kilometres out and needs a car; it has no public transport connection to the city at all. The Kilianseiche in Schesslitz, fifteen kilometres north, is the opposite case: roughly twenty-five minutes on the regional bus from Bamberg ZOB. The three field trees are separate trips again: the Pödeldorf lime about four kilometres east, the Dörfleins maple about seven north, the Unterhaid lime about twelve west.

Five stand in the open with no gate: a footpath, two roadside verges, a road junction in Schesslitz and a quiet country road near Teuchatz. The Buger Hof linden stands at the edge of a riverside hotel's grounds; the view from the public towpath is free, and whether the ground directly beneath it is open was not confirmed. The maple at Dörfleins and the limes at Unterhaid and Pödeldorf stand on farmland; no source confirms a path to the trunk, so expect to view them from the field edge.

faq.q: Why do so few of Bamberg's protected trees carry an age?
faq.a: The city's Naturdenkmal register records a number, a name, a location and the fact of protection, nothing about planting dates or ring counts, and that covers four of the nine; the district's list, which protects the Kilianseiche in Schesslitz and the three field trees at Dörfleins, Unterhaid and Pödeldorf, records even less. The exception, the Great Lime of Teuchatz, is documented separately in published dendrology surveys that give an actual girth history, which is where its rough age estimate comes from.

trees.name: The Lindens of the Ottobrunnen

location.address: Opposite the Ottobrunnen, off the Bamberger Weg footpath, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free. Stands right beside a public footpath (Bamberger Weg) in the wooded Berggebiet above Wildensorg; reachable on foot or by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg Mitte (lines 910/913), then a short uphill walk.
trees.transport: Bus to Wildensorg Mitte (lines 910/913) then approx. 10-15 min uphill on foot; no train option.
trees.story:
Two trees, one monument. Bamberg's natural monument register lists number three as "2 Linden am Ottobrunnen", a pair of small-leaved limes on the wooded hillside above Wildensorg, and protects them as a single entry rather than as two trees that happen to stand together. They face the Ottobrunnen, a spring on the Bamberger Weg, the footpath that climbs out of the city into the Berggebiet. The well carries the name of Otto of Bamberg, the bishop who died in 1139. That name belongs to the water and to the ground around it, and nothing on record attaches these two limes to him, so the story stops where the sources do.

A lime beside a well is one of the older arrangements in German village life, the tree marking the water and the meeting place at once. Whether that is why this pair is here, nobody wrote down. What is written down is the protection: both fall under the city ordinance of November 1995, amended in 2007, which means neither can be felled or cut back at anyone's convenience.

Go for the walk rather than for the trees alone. The path is wooded, the climb is short, and the pair stands at the top of it with the spring opposite.

Neither lime has been dated and neither trunk has been measured. If you get up there with a tape, tell us what they come to.
trees.how_to_recognise: The pair of limes stands opposite a spring right where the Bamberger Weg footpath emerges from the trees; there is no other planted pair nearby.

trees.name: The Oak of the Teufelsgraben

location.address: Teufelsgraben, southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free, standing along the Teufelsgraben path/street on the Wildensorg hillside, southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium school; OpenStreetMap independently tags it as a roadside tree rather than inside a fenced plot. Not on school grounds; the register describes it as standing 'southwest of' the school, not on its site.
trees.transport: Uphill from central Bamberg in Wildensorg/Berggebiet; reachable by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg, then on foot.
trees.story:
The address is the Devil's Ditch. Teufelsgraben is a lane running down the Wildensorg hillside southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium, and the oak stands on the verge of it, in the open, with nothing between it and the lane. It is not a school tree. The register places it southwest of the building rather than on the site, and you reach it without passing a gate or asking anyone.

Worth knowing before you go, a second protected oak stands close by, and that one is inside a garden plot, which the register says in as many words. The tree on this page is the one out on the bank above the lane, standing alone.

It is a pedunculate oak, the species that hangs its acorns on long stalks and holds its leaves almost stalkless against the twig, which is the reverse of the sessile oak it gets confused with. Bamberg protects it as natural monument 5, under the ordinance the city passed in November 1995 and amended in 2007, so it cannot be felled or cut back at anyone's convenience.

The rest of the hillside is worth the climb with it. The Ottobrunnen limes and the lime at the old Rothof are both within a couple of kilometres on foot.

What nobody has recorded is how old this oak is or how thick. Oaks carry centuries without advertising them. If you have measured it, tell us.

trees.how_to_recognise: A lone oak on the open verge of the Teufelsgraben lane, standing free of any fence or garden. A second protected oak on the same register sits inside a garden plot nearby and is not this one.

trees.name: The Linden of the Buger Hof

location.address: Am Regnitzufer 1, Bug, Bamberg (beside the Buger Hof hotel-restaurant, on the Regnitz riverbank)

trees.access: Free to view from the Regnitz riverside path; the address (Am Regnitzufer 1) is the Buger Hof hotel-restaurant, so the tree stands at the edge of its grounds beside the public riverbank. Whether a visitor needs to be a guest to stand directly beneath it, versus viewing it from the towpath, was not separately confirmed this pass; flagged so a future pass or reader can settle it.
trees.transport: In Bug, on the Regnitz river a few km south of central Bamberg; reachable by bike path along the river or by car/bus toward Bug.
trees.story:
Its official name is a house number. Bamberg's register of natural monuments lists entry 10 as "1 Linde am Regnitzufer 1", and the address it is named after is the Buger Hof, a hotel and restaurant on the riverbank in Bug, the village district a few kilometres upstream of the cathedral. The tree is a small-leaved lime and it stands at the edge of that ground, where the garden meets the Regnitz.

So the access is an open question and it is better said than glossed over. The lime is in full view from the public path along the river, the one walkers and cyclists use to get out of Bamberg southwards, and that view is free to anyone. Whether the last few metres underneath it are open to a passer-by or belong to the terrace is something we have not been able to settle. Look from the path. Ask inside if you want to stand under the crown.

Riverbank suits a lime better than almost anywhere else in a city: water at the root, open light on the water side, and no pavement compacting the ground over it. The city has protected this one since the ordinance of November 1995.

No age is recorded for it and no one has put a tape around the trunk. If you know either number, or whether the ground beneath it is open, tell us.

photo.attribution: Stephan van Helden, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: The lime at the corner of the Buger Hof's riverside grounds, visible from the towpath where the garden meets the Regnitz.

trees.name: The Linden of the Old Rothof

location.address: Wildensorger Straße, at the site of the former Rothof estate, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free. The historic Rothof estate building itself was demolished in the mid-1960s (per infranken.de reporting on the site's later redevelopment as a municipal water reservoir); the property is no longer a private residence, and OpenStreetMap tags the tree as a roadside lime on Wildensorger Straße rather than inside a fenced garden. Treated as publicly reachable on that basis.
trees.transport: Uphill from central Bamberg in Wildensorg/Berggebiet; reachable by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg, then on foot.
trees.story:
The estate this tree is named after was pulled down in the middle of the 1960s. The Rothof stood on the Wildensorger Straße, up on the hillside west of Bamberg; the buildings went, and the ground eventually went to the city's drinking water, which is what the site holds now. The lime is still there, on what the register calls the northern boundary of the property. A boundary line with nothing left to divide.

That whole history is in the register's own wording. Natural monument 6, protected under the city ordinance of November 1995: "1 Linde am ehemaligen Rothof, nördliche Grundstücksgrenze". One lime at the former Rothof, northern property line. The farm is described in the past tense and the tree is not.

It is a small-leaved lime and it stands by the road, which is the useful part for anyone walking up. There is no gate, no garden and no permission to ask. The hillside route that takes in the Teufelsgraben oak and the pair of limes at the Ottobrunnen passes within about a kilometre and a half of it, so all three fit into one afternoon on foot.

How much of the Rothof this lime actually saw is the open question. Nobody has dated it and nobody has measured the trunk. If you have, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: A lime standing alone by the road on Wildensorger Strasse, on open ground where the Rothof once stood. There is no building left to mark the spot beyond the tree itself.

trees.name: The Great Lime of Teuchatz
trees.age_estimate: roughly 350 to 400 years, if a local legend about its planting holds

location.address: On the road (Kreisstrasse) from Teuchatz to Burggrub, Markt Heiligenstadt in Oberfranken, Landkreis Bamberg

trees.access: Free. Stands immediately beside the public road between Teuchatz and Burggrub, no gate or fence.
trees.transport: About 16 km from Bamberg centre in the Fraenkische Schweiz, roughly 25 minutes by car. No rail (the branch line to Heiligenstadt closed in 1968) and no confirmed public bus reaches Teuchatz, so this one needs a car rather than the city's transit network.
trees.story:
Local legend ties this lime to the Thirty Years' War: soldiers from the Swedish army, the story goes, were buried here in the 1630s and the tree grew from their graves. Nobody can prove the burial, but the tree's girth roughly fits that timeline, tracked at 770 centimetres round in 1990 and 822 centimetres in 2008, which is honest grounds for guessing it is nearing four centuries old if the legend holds and nothing more precise if it does not.

The trunk is thick enough that a separate story grew up around it too, that it is really three trees fused into one. Look closely and the case falls apart. Dendrologists who have studied the tree describe a single continuous trunk, heavily buttressed and studded with burls at the base rather than three obvious stems. What has needed real intervention is the crown, cut back hard in recent years and now held together with steel cables above the point, about four metres up, where it forks into several broad limbs. It once spread 26 metres wide.

Teuchatz has no railway; the branch line that served it closed in 1968, and no confirmed bus makes the trip either. Getting here from Bamberg means a car and about 25 minutes on quiet roads, at the end of which the tree stands directly on the roadside with nothing between the pavement and the trunk. A war grave for a legend and a trunk that still argues about how many trees it started as.
trees.how_to_recognise: The one large lime standing directly on the roadside between Teuchatz and Burggrub, its crown visibly cut back and braced with steel cables; there is no other tree of its size on this stretch of road.

trees.name: The Kilianseiche of Schesslitz

location.address: Junction of Hauptstrasse and the road to the cemetery, near the Ziegelmuehle, Schesslitz

trees.story:
Most protected trees in the Bamberg district get a number. This one got a name. The district's 2009 ordinance lists natural monument 61 as the Kilianseiche, Kilian's oak, standing where the Hauptstrasse in Schesslitz turns off toward the cemetery. A plain oak a few hundred metres away, number 62, is listed simply as an oak.

The name is nearly all the register gives. It records no species, no girth, no height and no age, so even calling this an oak rests on the name rather than on a survey. Which oak it is, and how old, are questions this page cannot answer yet.

The name does point somewhere. The parish church in Schesslitz is dedicated to Saint Kilian, and the bus from Bamberg stops at a halt called Kilianskirche. Whether the tree was named for the church, or for some older reason, no source we have found says, so we will not invent a story for it.

Then the caveat that matters most. The only photograph of the tree we can find is an old upload to the Panoramio photo site, taken sixteen metres from the register's point, and there is nothing recent. The ordinance still protects it, but we cannot show you dated proof that it stands.

Schesslitz is about fifteen kilometres north of Bamberg, roughly twenty-five minutes on the regional bus. If you make the trip, tell us whether Kilian's oak is still at its junction, and if you know your oaks, which kind it is.

trees.access: Free. Stands at a road junction on the way to the village cemetery, on public ground as far as the register wording shows ('an der Abzweigung der Hauptstrasse zum Friedhof'); not checked against OSM tags.
trees.transport: About 15 km north of Bamberg. Regional bus from Bamberg ZOB to the Schesslitz Kilianskirche stop, roughly 25 minutes (line 969 in the 2024 VGN timetable; check the current one), then on foot to the junction of the Hauptstrasse and the road to the cemetery.
trees.notes: Register only, one source (Bavarian LfU point layer ND-03526 plus the Landkreis ordinance reproduced on de.wikipedia). The register gives NO species, girth, height or age: 'Kilianseiche' means 'Kilian's oak' so oak is inferred from the name only, not from a record; call it an oak and leave the species a question for readers. Alive: weak. lifecheck returned RECENT 2025-01-06 but that match was a beer-glass photograph 16 m away, not the tree, so it proves nothing; the only tree image is an old Panoramio upload on Commons. Page should say the register lists it and ask readers to confirm it stands. Pin is the register's tree-level point and a geotagged Commons photograph sits 16 m from it, so confirmed is defensible but not checked against aerial imagery. Photograph in reach (Commons category). Why it is worth a stop: it is one of the few named (not just numbered) monuments in the district, named for Saint Kilian, the patron of Schesslitz's parish church (the church's St. Kilian dedication is visible in nearby Commons file names; no tree history sourced, writer must not invent one). Same ordinance also lists no. 62 'Eiche' at the Demmelsdorfer Strasse / Altenbach junction (49.97416, 11.03862, Flurstueck 536), about 300 m away, a plain unnamed oak, not delivered. Transport time from the VGN line 969 timetable (valid from 10.12.2023): Sunday departure Bamberg ZOB 11:34, Schesslitz Kilianskirche 12:00, about 26 minutes; the timetable warns of changes from 01.08.2024. Day-trip boundary: within 30 minutes by public transport, so it sits on the Bamberg page with its real place name.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: at the junction where the Hauptstrasse in Schesslitz turns off toward the cemetery, near the Ziegelmuehle. An unnamed protected oak stands 300 metres away on the Demmelsdorfer Strasse.

trees.verify_notes: Register plus ordinance (one official source, owner of the ground's regulator) plus 10 Commons photographs dated Feb 2024, so alive as of 2024-02-17. Register point 49.93652,10.86397; photographer GPS fixes cluster at 49.93637-49.93642, 10.86374-10.86391, within about 15 m of it, so the pin is confirmed by GPS at the tree. Ordinance names only 'Ahorn' (genus Acer), no girth, height or age; species left as a question for readers. Official protection reason, quoted from the Wikipedia list's Schutzgrund column: the tree 'bereichert und prägt durch seine Schönheit und Dominanz das Ortsbild' (enriches and shapes the village scene by its beauty and dominance). Ordinance sets a 10 m protected zone around it. Photograph in reach: Commons category above (Stephan van Helden, CC BY-SA 4.0, user Plozessor). Another register oak (ND-04404, Kilianstraße cul-de-sac, already a lead) stands about 700 m away in the same village, but is not a delivered tree. Not a spectacular-age claim: do not call it old. The register has no vitality field; 2024 photographs are the life evidence.
trees.story:
In April 2010 the district of Bamberg passed a law about one maple. The ordinance is titled for the Ahorn nördlich von Dörfleins, the maple north of Dörfleins, and it covers a single tree on a single field parcel, number 4050, with a protected zone ten metres around it.

The reason it gives is not age. In the official wording, the tree enriches and shapes the look of the village through its beauty and its dominance. That is a planning office saying, as plainly as planning offices ever do, that this is the tree people in Dörfleins see when they look north across the fields.

The paperwork stops there. It records no species beyond maple, no girth, no height and no planting date, so we will not call it old and we will not guess at a number. What we can show is that it stands: a photographer recorded it for Wikimedia Commons on 17 February 2024, ten pictures taken within about fifteen metres of the trunk.

Dörfleins is part of Hallstadt, about seven kilometres north of Bamberg's centre. A protected oak stands about 700 metres away in the same village. No source we found says whether a footpath reaches the maple itself; the 2024 photographs were taken from the field edge, and that is where to stand.

Sycamore, Norway maple or field maple: the register does not say which, and nobody has dated it. If you know either answer, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the maple standing in the field north of Dörfleins, on parcel 4050, inside a protected zone of ten metres. The village's other protected tree, an oak, is about 700 metres away.

trees.story:
The official description of this tree runs to two words: 1 Linde, one lime. Bavaria's register of natural monuments lists it as ND-03903, the Bamberg district's list as number 48, on land parcel 669 at Unterhaid.

Where the record gets specific is the address. The lime stands about 200 metres north of the railway underpass, in what the register calls a Baumfeld, a tree field, on the east side of a farm track laid out when the fields here were consolidated. It is a precise way to find a tree and a thin way to describe one.

Everything a visitor usually asks about is missing. No species beyond lime, no girth, no height, no age. On Wikimedia Commons its photographs sit in a category called the big lime of Unterhaid, but that is somebody's label rather than a measurement, and we will not repeat it as one.

What those photographs do settle is that the tree was alive on 18 March 2023, and that the camera stood within about six metres of the register's point, so the pin is good.

Unterhaid belongs to Oberhaid, about twelve kilometres west of Bamberg's centre. The farm track beside the tree field is the likely way in, though no source we found confirms it, so treat this as a stop on a country walk rather than a destination in itself.

Nobody has dated this lime or named its species. If you have stood under it, tell us what you found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: in the tree field on the east side of the farm track, about 200 metres north of the railway underpass at Unterhaid.

trees.transport: Pödeldorf is about 4 km east of Bamberg centre. Public transport not checked.
trees.verify_notes: Register (one official source) plus two Commons photographs dated 11 Sept 2023, so alive as of 2023-09. Photograph geotag (49.90913-49.90914, 10.99555) is the camera position about 36 m south-west of the register point (49.90946, 10.99578), so the exact trunk is not fixed: kept approximate, not confirmed. Register gives genus only (Linde), no girth, height or age. Photograph in reach: Commons category above. Weak on remarkability: a protected rise-top linden with no sourced story; flagged. The register has no vitality field.
trees.story:
Bavaria's register gives directions to this lime the way a farmer would: on the high ground between Pödeldorf and Naisa, about 50 metres east of the edge of the village. It is natural monument ND-03734, number 46 on the Bamberg district's list, on land parcel 105.

That sentence of directions is most of what the register says. It names the tree only as a lime, with no species, no girth, no height and no age, and no source we found tells its history. What it has is a place: open ground, just where the village stops and the fields toward Naisa begin.

The proof of life is recent enough to trust. Two photographs on Wikimedia Commons, taken on 11 September 2023 and titled with its register number, show it standing. The camera that took them stood about 36 metres south-west of the register's point, though, which means neither the photographs nor the register fix the exact trunk, and our pin is marked approximate for that reason.

Pödeldorf is about four kilometres east of Bamberg's centre, close enough to make this a short outing from the city. No source confirms a path to the tree, so expect to view it from the field edge.

Nobody has published an age or the species of this lime. If you walk up to it and know which lime it is, or have a tape measure in your pocket, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime on the rise between Pödeldorf and Naisa, about 50 metres east of where the houses of Pödeldorf end.
